rci8_quality_checking.detail: Visual inspection by trained operators using ENIGMA QC protocols; Euler value used to assess motion; 8 participants excluded based on visual inspection for motion, poor image quality, or aberrant FreeSurfer processing.
rci8_quality_checking.supporting_text: Data were visually inspected by a trained operator (DJR) and research staff (KAT) to ensure accuracy. The ENIGMA quality control protocols were also used (Thompson et al., 2020). Three participants (comparison group) demonstrated significantly aberrant FreeSurfer processing (such as failed boundary identification) and they were excluded from analyses. Five additional participants (three comparison, two FASD) were excluded on the basis of motion during the visual inspection of the images or for being an extreme outlier in regional volume metrics. To assess for group differences in within-scanner motion in the remaining participants, we used the Euler value (Dale et al., 1999) averaged across hemispheres.

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa7_association_analysis: Group differences in volume z-scores were tested with independent samples t-tests. Uncorrected exploratory Pearson correlations were used to examine relationships between subcortical volume z-scores and neurocognitive measures (IQ, D-KEFS) separately within the FASD and comparison groups.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa8_key_findings_brief: Youth with FASD showed a greater number of atypically small subcortical volumes than controls, and in the FASD group, smaller caudate volumes were associated with lower IQ and executive function.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa9_key_findings_detailed: Compared to 39 controls, 47 youth with FASD had significantly smaller mean z-scores for subcortical volumes in 6 of 7 regions, with the largest effects in bilateral caudate and hippocampi (d > 0.8). A greater proportion of the FASD group had at least one small volume (89% vs 72%). Exploratory analyses revealed that for the FASD group, smaller bilateral caudate volumes were positively correlated with IQ and cognitive flexibility. In contrast, for the comparison group, higher IQ was associated with smaller volumes in the putamen and pallidum.

caa10_key_limitations.answer: The study's limitations include a non-generalizable, convenience sample (FASD vs. controls); unmeasured confounding from polysubstance exposure and socioeconomic status (SES); racial disparities between groups; a narrow focus on subcortical regions; and systematic negative shifts in z-scores, likely due to methodological differences between the study's data acquisition/processing and that of the heterogeneous datasets used to create the CentileBrain normative model.
caa10_key_limitations.supporting_text: There are several limitations of this study... Participants in this study were recruited based on a history of PAE or being typically-developing... Polysubstance exposure is common... We did not have access to detailed information about tobacco exposures... there was a higher proportion of White participants in the comparison group vs. the FASD group, potentially introducing bias... we focused our examination on subcortical regions of interest... It is also important to note that we found systematically smaller norm-corrected subcortical volumes in our participants, likely reflecting differences in image acquisition and processing differences with the heterogeneous samples used by CentileBrain, which represents a limitation of this study.

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa11_application_notes: The study highlights the value of applying a pre-trained, large-scale normative model (CentileBrain) to a smaller, single-site clinical dataset. This approach allows for the quantification of brain anomalies at the individual level, which can reveal clinical-biological associations that may be obscured in traditional case-control analyses.

general_note_part.gn1_general_notes: A key finding and limitation is that even the healthy comparison group showed systematically smaller-than-expected subcortical volumes (i.e., negative mean z-scores) in several regions. The authors attribute this to methodological heterogeneity between their single-site HCP-style pipeline and the multi-source, multi-pipeline data that constitutes the CentileBrain normative model. This suggests that while group *differences* are interpretable, the absolute z-scores from applying this pre-trained model may be systematically biased.
